idiom_name: compile-time confinement: ownership plus Send/Sync, std::thread::scope, thread_local! macro
implementation_notes: Rust's type system enforces what other languages document: a value is confined to its thread unless it is `Send`, and shared access requires `Sync`, so a non-thread-safe type such as `Rc<T>`/`RefCell<T>` simply cannot cross a thread boundary - the compiler rejects it. Within a thread, ownership makes stack confinement the default (the borrow checker stops a reference escaping into a longer-lived context), and `std::thread::scope` (Rust 1.63) lets spawned threads borrow non-'static local data with a guaranteed join, replacing the classic thread-per-task workaround. For genuinely per-thread state, the `thread_local!` macro provides a `LocalKey<T>` (`with` hands out only `&T`, so `Cell`/`RefCell` provide mutation). The hand-off structures are still needed when data must move between threads - there you transfer ownership through channels or share behind `Arc<Mutex<_>>` - and that is the same pattern, now checked.
pitfalls: thread_local! values with drop-tracking need lazy initialization machinery (the macro's const-init opt-out avoids it) and on Windows synchronization inside TLS destructors is documented as deadlock-prone.
`Arc<Mutex<_>>` makes sharing legal, not confined: smuggling an `Rc` through raw pointers or a wrong `unsafe impl Send` defeats the guarantee and is undefined behaviour, not a compiler error.
For scoped threads, joining and `thread::scope` return before a thread's thread-local destructors may have finished (documented), so cleanup must not assume completion ordering.
